opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I like to frame it is this: as a community we've spent decades learning from images, text, audio, video, graphs. Those are the classic modalities. But over the last few years we've produced millions of trained neural networks, sitting on model hubs, in checkpoints, in hyperparameter sweeps. Each of those weight sets is a compressed artifact of a training process. It encodes something about the data it saw, the architecture, the optimizer, even the random seed. So my question was, why don't we treat that population of models as a dataset in its own right? Why not learn from weights the way we learn from pixels?

That's what we've been calling the model zoo direction, or more broadly weight-space learning. We build large, structured collections of trained models, varying things like initialization, hyperparameters, and datasets, and save checkpoints along the training trajectories. Then we ask what you can learn just by looking at the parameters, without running the model on data.

It turns out you can learn quite a lot. From weights alone you can predict a model's test accuracy, its generalization gap, which hyperparameters were used, sometimes properties of the training data. Early on we did this with simple statistics of the weights, and that already worked surprisingly well. Then we moved to representation learning: self-supervised methods, a hyper-representation, where you train an encoder on model weights and get an embedding space where each point is a whole neural network.

Then it gets really interesting, because if you have a good representation you can also go generative. You can decode from that latent space and sample new weights. We've shown you can generate models that serve as better initializations than random ones, or that fall into particular regions of performance. So you go from analyzing models to synthesizing them.

There are real challenges that make weights different from images. The big one is symmetry. You can permute the neurons in a hidden layer, and with the matching permutation in the next layer, you get a functionally identical network with a completely different parameter vector. So the input space is full of equivalences, and your learning method has to respect them, through augmentation, canonicalization, or architectures that are equivariant by design. The other challenge is scale and heterogeneity. A ResNet and a transformer don't share a fixed input shape, so we've worked on tokenizing weights, breaking them into chunks so a sequence model can handle varying architectures and larger models.

The long-term vision is that weights become a first-class modality, and that you could eventually have something like a foundation model over neural networks themselves. You'd use it to audit models on a hub, detect a backdoor or a poorly trained checkpoint, transfer knowledge between models, or generate a starting point for a new task instead of training from scratch every time. Given how much compute we spend producing these models, it seems wasteful not to learn from them.

r001.rationale: It treats trained weights as a dataset and compares learning from weights to learning from pixels, but does not compare this to language modeling over text.

r002.rationale: It discusses transferring knowledge between models, but does not raise model-to-model translation as an analogue of language translation.

r003.rationale: It describes generating better initializations and a starting point for a new task instead of training from scratch, communicating that learning from weights could speed task-specific model creation.

r004.rationale: It proposes auditing models and detecting backdoors or poor training, but does not specify analyzing a previously unseen network with no prior knowledge about it.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. So the way we got into this is actually fairly simple. Everybody in the field spends enormous amounts of compute training neural networks, and what comes out at the end is a set of weights. Those weights are the thing we care about, we deploy them, we fine-tune them, we share them on Hugging Face. But almost nobody treats them as data in their own right. We look at the training curves, we look at the accuracy, and then the weights disappear into a checkpoint file.

And our question was, well, what if you take those checkpoints and you consider them as samples from some distribution? If you train a thousand small CNNs on CIFAR with different seeds, different hyperparameters, different optimizers, you get a thousand points in weight space. That's a dataset. We call these model zoos. And once you have a dataset, the obvious thing for a deep learning person to do is to learn representations on it.

So the first thing we did was quite literal. We trained something like an autoencoder over the flattened weight vectors, and we asked, does the latent space carry any information? And it turns out it does. You can predict from the weights alone, without ever running the model on a single input, things like what the test accuracy is, how far along in training the model is, what the learning rate was, whether it was trained with Adam or SGD, sometimes even which activation function was used. That was surprising to us, because if you just look at the raw numbers it looks like noise.

Now, the interesting part, and the part that makes this harder than images or text, are the symmetries. Weight space has a lot of structure that is purely an artifact of how we parameterize networks. If you permute the neurons in a hidden layer and permute the corresponding rows and columns in the adjacent weight matrices, you get a functionally identical network, but a completely different weight vector. So two models that compute exactly the same function can be very far apart in Euclidean distance. If you ignore that, your representation learning is fighting against something that isn't actually signal. So a big part of the work is designing architectures or augmentations that are either invariant or equivariant to those permutations, and to things like scaling symmetries with ReLU networks. You can do this with augmentation, essentially showing the model many permuted versions of the same network so it learns to ignore that, or you can bake it into the architecture, which is where a lot of the community has moved recently with things like neural functionals and graph-based approaches that treat the network as a graph of neurons and edges.

And then there's the question of what you actually do with these representations beyond analysis. One direction that I find exciting is generative. If you can encode weights into a latent space, you can also decode from that latent space, and that means you can sample new weights. So instead of training from scratch, you sample an initialization from the learned distribution that is already in a good region, and you fine-tune from there. In our experiments that gives you models that are not random, they already have reasonable performance in zero-shot, and they reach good performance much faster. It's a form of learned prior over networks. And more broadly I think of it as a kind of hypernetwork, but one that is grounded in a population of real trained models rather than having to learn everything from the task loss.

The other direction is diagnostics. If you can read properties off the weights, you can in principle look at a model and say, this looks overfit, or this looks like it was trained on something similar to that other model, or this has been backdoored, without having access to the training data. For model marketplaces, for auditing, for understanding what's going on inside a model, that's very attractive.

I should be honest about the limitations. Most of the work so far is on small models, and the question of whether this scales to transformers with billions of parameters is still open. The dimensionality is brutal, and the symmetries get more complicated. But my intuition is that the weights are the most direct artifact of what a network has learned, and it would be strange if that artifact were not itself learnable. We spend all this effort learning from data that we did not create, and here we have data that we created ourselves, in vast quantities, and we are just now starting to look at it.

r001.rationale: The response calls trained weights a dataset and discusses learning representations, but does not compare this to language modeling over text.

r002.rationale: It does not raise translating between models as an analogue of language translation.

r003.rationale: It describes sampling a learned initialization and fine-tuning it to reach good performance faster, communicating that learned weights could speed up creating task-specific weights.

r004.rationale: It proposes diagnosing a model from its weights without training data, but does not establish that the network is previously unseen or that the analyst has no prior knowledge of it.

astra-6.text:
I think the interesting shift is to stop looking at a neural network only as a function that makes predictions and start looking at the trained network itself as a data point. Those weights are the result of a learning process. They contain information about the data the network has seen, the task it was trained on, and how it was optimized. So can we learn from a population of trained networks, just as we learn from a collection of images or documents?

That gives us a representation learning problem where the input modality is the weights. We would like to map those weights into an embedding that captures meaningful properties of the model. For example, could we predict how well a network will perform without running a full evaluation? Could we identify models that are useful for transfer learning? And if we can decode those representations back into weights, could we generate a useful initialization for a new task?

The challenge is that weight space has symmetries. You can permute neurons, adjust the corresponding connections, and get exactly the same function, even though the weight vectors look different. So simply flattening the parameters and measuring their distance is not enough. The representation has to capture something about what the network has learned, rather than just how its parameters happen to be arranged. That’s what makes this an interesting modality in its own right.

r001.rationale: It compares learning from trained networks to learning from collections of images or documents, but does not specifically draw the analogy to language modeling over a text corpus.

r002.rationale: It discusses mapping weights into embeddings and decoding them back into weights, but does not raise translating between models as an analogue of language translation.

r003.rationale: It asks whether decoding representations into weights could generate a useful initialization for a new task, which communicates using learned weights to accelerate creating weights for that task.

r004.rationale: It asks about predicting performance and identifying models for transfer, but does not propose analyzing an unseen network with no prior knowledge about it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the interesting shift is to stop looking at a trained neural network only as a function that maps inputs to outputs, and start looking at the network itself as a data point. During training, information about the data and the task gets encoded in the weights. So can we learn to read that representation?

Imagine you have a collection of networks trained with different initializations, on different datasets, or with different hyperparameters. Each network becomes one example, and its weights become the input to another learning system. You can then ask whether that system can predict properties of a network, like its performance, or learn a representation that helps you generate useful weights for a new model.

But weights have some peculiar properties. For example, you can permute neurons, adjust the corresponding connections, and get exactly the same function, even though the weight vector looks different. So simply treating weights like an ordinary feature vector misses some of the structure.

That’s what makes this an interesting representation-learning problem: how do we capture what a network has learned while accounting for the different ways that knowledge can be represented in its parameters?

r001.rationale: The response treats networks as data points for another learning system, but does not compare a corpus of network weights to a text corpus or language modeling.

r002.rationale: It does not raise translating between models or compare that task to language translation.

r003.rationale: It asks whether the learned representation could help generate useful weights for a new model, which communicates accelerating weight creation.

r004.rationale: It mentions predicting properties of networks, but does not describe analyzing a previously unseen network with no prior knowledge about it.
